disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear minor to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors or mental acts focused on these concerns and causing significant distress or impairment. Onset is typically in adolescence and early adulthood, often in the context of heightened social comparison, bullying, or appearance-focused environments, and the course is usually chronic without treatment, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress. BDD is distinct from normal appearance dissatisfaction by the intensity of preoccupation, the degree of functional impairment, and the often poor insight or delusional conviction about the perceived defect; it is differentiated from eating disorders by the focus on specific body parts or features rather than weight or shape overall. Comorbidities commonly include depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, and OCD-spectrum conditions, and individuals frequently engage in excessive grooming, mirror checking, reassurance seeking, or camouflaging behaviors, as well as seeking cosmetic procedures that rarely alleviate distress.

narrative.personality: Imad is a pragmatic, introverted tinkerer who channels his restlessness into solitary hikes and DIY tech projects while quietly planning for a more responsible future role at work.
narrative.stressor: Imad’s concerns about his appearance began to intensify in his final year of high school, when classmates repeatedly made offhand jokes about his looks and he started comparing himself to more athletic peers during gym and on social media. After graduation he moved into a physically demanding warehouse job, where working alongside older, more muscular coworkers in a hot, fluorescently lit environment made him acutely self-conscious about how he looked in his uniform. As he took on more responsibility and talked about pursuing certification, he became increasingly anxious that his appearance would undermine how seriously supervisors and peers viewed him, leading him to spend more and more time before and after shifts trying to “fix” how he looked. The mounting time he devoted to these routines began to interfere with his punctuality, cut into his sleep, and made him turn down social invitations and even extra shifts, prompting him to seek psychiatric help when he realized his attempts to manage his concerns were starting to jeopardize both his job and his plans for advancement.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m spending so much time on these little routines to fix how I look before work that it’s starting to mess with my schedule and my life.”

narrative.personality: Clara is a highly organized, data-driven problem solver who channels her anxious energy into optimizing systems, staying physically active, and maintaining a polished, high-achieving image.
narrative.stressor: Clara’s preoccupation with her appearance deepened after she was promoted into a more visible operations role at her fast-growing tech firm, which required frequent presentations, video calls, and networking events. In this new position she felt constant pressure to embody the image of a polished, energetic leader, especially as younger, image-conscious colleagues and leadership emphasized “personal branding” and she saw carefully curated photos of herself and others circulating on the company’s internal channels and social media. Her longstanding tendency to channel worry into control and precision gradually shifted from purely work processes to scrutinizing specific aspects of how she looked in photos, mirrors, and video previews, and she began organizing her days around trying to manage what she saw as glaring flaws. Over time, this preoccupation started to erode her confidence in meetings, led her to avoid certain networking events, and strained her marriage as she sought repeated reassurance from her spouse, ultimately driving her to seek psychiatric care when she noticed that her worries about her appearance were consuming far more time and energy than her actual work responsibilities.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop obsessing over this one part of how I look, and it’s taking over my days and making work and social stuff really hard.”

narrative.personality: Kettia is an ambitious, detail-oriented auditor with a warm, community-focused side who balances demanding work with lively group activities and cultural interests.
narrative.stressor: For Kettia, concerns about her appearance had been background noise since adolescence, but they sharpened in her early thirties as she advanced to a senior auditor role and became more visible in client-facing engagements and professional photos for her firm’s website and community events. She began to fixate on perceived imperfections that she felt made her look unprofessional or older than her peers, especially when she saw candid photos from cultural festivals, fitness classes, and volunteer workshops posted online. Coming from a family and social circle where appearance, grooming, and comments about looking “put together” were common, she internalized a belief that these perceived flaws could undermine her credibility as a young Black professional woman in a conservative industry. Over time, the mental energy spent worrying about how she looked before client meetings and community presentations began to sap the enjoyment from activities she usually loved and made her increasingly hesitant to be photographed or attend social events, leading her to seek psychiatric evaluation when she realized these preoccupations were starting to interfere with both her career growth and her community involvement.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m constantly fixated on this one flaw in how I look, and it’s starting to make me dread going to events or being seen.”
